The Good:

  • All the features of Logitech's M570 and more minus the hassle of wireless

  • Plug and play

  • Tilt wheel and on-the-fly hardware-based DPI switching with indicator LED

The Bad:

  • Polished shiny surface is not for everyone and attracts a lot of grime

  • Quite rough trackball before break-in period

  • Only available via import

I was a user of the Logitech Trackman Marble, which is the first mouse I ever bought (I have never used a standard mouse in my laptops save for the trackpad) for about 4-5 years, but eventually I grew more and more frustrated about the lack of scroll wheel, and X-Mouse wasn't cutting it so I decided to get a trackball that had a scroll wheel.

My first option was the Logitech M570, which seemed very good but: 1. There were many comments about the switches dying off or misclicking after some time and Logitech customer support not responding in a favorable way. 2. I didn't like the idea of a wireless trackball. I barely move it if at all yet I would need batteries. Plus, Logitech's Unifying Receiver works at 2.4 GHz, which is the frequency of my WiFi router, and I didn't want to add additional interference so I thought maybe it isn't that good after all.

My second option was something from Kensington's trackball line. I thought the Orbit mouse with scroll ring would be good, but the lack of a proper scroll wheel with middle click turned me off. I definitely do not have the money for the SlimBlade so that wasn't an option.

I then found the Elecom M-XT1URBK, which seemed good enough, wired, multiple buttons, scroll + tilt wheel... but pretty much everyone says that to work correctly it needs the blue ball from the Logitech M570! I didn't want to buy a trackball to have to toss the stock ball away either so I crossed that one off my options.

Finally, I found about the Sanwa Supply line of trackballs. Comments were mixed, but mostly negative, especially on Japanese shopping portals, so I was somewhat hesitant to buy one of those. A commonly reported problem was that the ball didn't fit correctly, that it "sticked" or that the hardware acceleration was horrible. I did found out, however, that almost nobody had tried out the TB-44, only the TB-43 (wireless version), so I thought there may be some chance of it being better. I bought it on eBay, and 20 days later it arrived.

DESIGN

The Sanwa TB-44R is probably one of the best-looking trackballs available, with its metallic red/gray body with a highly sculpted shape not unlike a glove. There are three buttons apart from the left, right, and middle click (scroll wheel), two which by default work as a forward/backward button, and the third one is the DPI control, which persists among reboots and even disconnections. There's a nifty hidden red LED at the left of the secondary buttons that blinks when the DPI is changed, 1, 2, 3, and 4 times according to the DPI setting; 400, 800, 1200 and 1600 respectively.

The scroll wheel is a rubberized one, with silver sides. It's notched and does not freely spin. I should also note that although I couldn't find any information indicating it, the scroll wheel has a tilt function as well. Very nice.

The ball itself is a metallic red one, with some tone variation to it.

The two main buttons are powered by Omrom switches, and make a satisfying click. The rest of the buttons use HiMAKE switches and are very good as well. None of them during the two weeks I have been using them have sticked or misclicked.

The USB cable is pretty standard, though a bit on the thin side. The Trackman Marble's cable seems to be of a higher quality.

The underside has 4 rubber feet that do a good job keeping the trackball from moving.

FEATURES

The TB-44R is plug and play. Within seconds of getting it out of its box I was already using it. I did not download any of the drivers from the Sanwa website so I can't comment on that.

All the buttons except for the DPI one are remappable with your software of choice (e.g. X-Mouse).

There's no noticeable delay between the movement of the ball and the movement of the cursor. The DPI switch works on Windows, Mac and GNU/Linux without any software, and allows for fine movement or quick strokes. I have the default Windows cursor settings (sensitivity, acceleration, etc.) and I have the DPI in 1200 for general usage, while I reduce it to 800 for precision movements.

The scroll+tilt wheel is awesome, allowing to scroll vertically AND horizontally, unlike the Logitech M570.

PERFORMANCE

In web browsing this trackball is ideal, allowing pretty much any movement you could want without having to move all your hand around.

In document/file operation I usually had to tone down the DPI, otherwise I would misclick a lot. The back/forward buttons work with the Windows' File Explorer so that's an advantage there as well.

In professional use (digital audio workstation) the trackball performed better than the Trackman Marble, the tilt wheel being particularly useful with timeline-based editing. The DPI switch helped a lot, being able to precisely select and point controls while also being good for quick edits.

The highly sculpted shape fits my hand perfectly. All fingers have a resting place, and I feel my hand's less tired than with the Trackman Marble.

I don't game so I can't comment on that. I did try it out on Need for Speed World though, and for menu and car vinyl positioning/editing it worked pretty well.

Unlike other people, I did not find the hardware acceleration bad at all. At 1200 DPI the cursor glides effortlessly through an 1920x1080 screen without being uncontrollable.

As a first-timer to thumb trackballs it didn't felt strange or hard to control, and I pretty much have the hang of it now.

Does the ball spin? Well, if you just got it out of the box then no. It's somewhat rough especially coming from the Trackman Marble whose ball was very, very smooth.

After two weeks it keeps spinning for about a second with a swift thumb movement. It doesn't seem like an overtly long break-in period to me, and now it feels as smooth as any other good trackball.

I did not find any issues with the fit or surface of the ball.

Cleaning it is no problem. The ball pops out just as in the Logitech trackballs. There are three white (ceramic?) bearings underneath it along with the laser sensor. Remove the grime/dust around them and put it back in.

The metallic finish, while nice, does attract a lot of grime (and I don't even eat in the same room my computer is, ever), and I find myself cleaning it daily otherwise the grip gets worse.

CONCLUSION

Totally worth it. The tilt wheel functionality along with the hardware DPI switch make it a very worthy upgrade from the Logitech M570. Very happy with it, no problems so far. For non-gaming usage, I'd highly recommend it, especially if you like thumb trackballs.

SPECIFICATIONS

Official image

MSRP: ¥6,912

Color: Red (available in black [TB-44BK] and silver [TB-44S])

Interface: USB 1.1 HID specification compliant (compatible with USB 2.0 and 3.0)

Connector type: USB A

Resolution: 1600 / 1200 / 800 / 400 DPI

Sensor type: Laser

Buttons: Left and right click (Omrom switches), two side buttons (back/forward; HiMAKE switches), DPI switch button (HiMAKE), scroll wheel button (middle click; unknown brand)

Dimensions: 95mm (width) x 126.5mm (diameter) x 44mm (height)

Weight: 160g (5.64 oz)

Cable length and color: 1.5m (59 in) black cable

Box includes: Trackball (1), instruction manual (1; all in Japanese only)
